units.title: A pool skips the 30 ms connection setup
units.claim: A new connection costs the Ledger service about 30 ms (TLS handshake and authentication); the pool keeps connections open and lends them, so most requests skip that cost.

omission.reason: The reason for everything that follows.

units.title: The pool caps the service's connections
units.claim: The pool caps how many connections the service can hold, which protects the database from a traffic spike.
units.explanation: The second purpose of the pool; it leads into sizing.

units.title: 20 connections per instance, autoscaler capped at 18
units.claim: Each Ledger instance runs at most 20 connections, and the autoscaler is capped at 18 instances.
units.explanation: The sizing rule an operator needs.

units.title: Why the cap is 18 instances
units.claim: The database accepts 400 connections, 40 are reserved for migrations and administrators, which leaves room for 18 instances at 20 each.
units.explanation: Explains ku.pool-size; must sit with it.

omission.reason: Supporting arithmetic; if shown, it stays with the sizing rule.

units.title: A bigger pool helps only while requests wait
units.claim: Raising the pool size only helps while requests are waiting for a connection.
units.explanation: The condition on using pool size as a lever.

units.title: Past CPU saturation, more connections slow every query
units.claim: Once the database CPU is saturated, more connections make every query slower.
units.explanation: Limits ku.bigger-pool: on the same card.

omission.reason: Without it a bigger pool reads as a general fix.

units.title: Peak sizing keeps idle connections at night
units.claim: A pool sized for peak traffic holds idle connections at night, which costs database memory but nothing else.

units.title: Borrowing waits at most 2 seconds, then POOL_EXHAUSTED
units.claim: A request waits at most 2 seconds to borrow a connection before it fails with POOL_EXHAUSTED.
units.explanation: The wait limit and the error callers see.

units.title: The wait is shorter than the 5-second deadline on purpose
units.claim: The wait limit is deliberately shorter than the 5-second request deadline, so the caller can still return a clear error.
units.explanation: Explains ku.borrow-wait; must sit with it.

omission.reason: Supporting; if shown, it stays with the wait limit.

units.title: Every query times out after 3 seconds
units.claim: Each query has a statement timeout of 3 seconds, set with SET statement_timeout = '3s' when the connection opens.

units.title: Except migrations
units.claim: The statement timeout does not apply to migrations, which run on their own reserved connections without a limit.
units.explanation: Limits ku.statement-timeout: on the same card.

units.title: Transactions stay under 500 ms
units.claim: A long transaction holds its connection for its whole duration, so the team keeps transactions under 500 ms.
units.explanation: A team rule that follows from how the pool lends connections.

units.title: Connections idle over 60 seconds are checked before lending
units.claim: Before lending a connection idle for more than 60 seconds, the pool runs SELECT 1 to check it still works.

units.title: A connection that fails the check is replaced
units.claim: A connection that fails the check is closed and replaced, and the request gets a fresh one.

omission.reason: Implied by a health check; may be folded into ku.idle-check's card.

units.title: A failover drains and refills the whole pool
units.claim: During a database failover every open connection breaks at once, so the pool is drained and refilled from the new primary.

units.title: Errors for up to about 4 seconds until refilled
units.claim: Until the pool is refilled, requests may see POOL_EXHAUSTED errors for up to about 4 seconds.
units.explanation: Limits ku.failover-drain: on the same card.

omission.reason: Without it the failover reads as invisible to callers.

units.title: Refilling is limited to 5 connections per second per instance
units.claim: Refilling is limited to 5 new connections per second per instance.

units.title: Why the refill is slowed
units.claim: The limit keeps 18 instances reconnecting together from overloading the new primary.
units.explanation: Explains ku.refill-rate; must sit with it.

omission.reason: Supporting; if shown, it stays with the refill limit.

units.title: Borrowed over 10 seconds: logged as a possible leak
units.claim: A connection borrowed for more than 10 seconds is logged as a possible leak, with the stack trace of the code that borrowed it.

units.title: A leaked connection is never taken back by force
units.claim: The pool does not take a leaked connection back by force, because the code holding it may still be using it.
units.explanation: Limits ku.leak-log: detection only, on the same card.

units.title: Most leaks come from early returns on error paths
units.claim: Most leaks the team has found came from error paths that returned early without releasing the connection.

units.title: Leak warnings are reviewed weekly
units.claim: Leak warnings are reviewed every week, and a leak that comes back gets a ticket for the team that owns the code.

units.title: Three gauges: in use, idle, waiting
units.claim: The pool exports three gauges: connections in use, idle connections, and requests waiting to borrow.

omission.reason: May be folded into the alert card.

units.title: On-call is paged after 30 seconds of waiting
units.claim: An alert pages the on-call engineer when requests have been waiting for more than 30 seconds in a row.

units.title: A sustained queue usually means slow queries, not a small pool
units.claim: A sustained queue usually means slow queries rather than a pool that is too small, so the runbook starts with the slowest statements, not the pool size.
units.explanation: The diagnosis rule, with its qualifier.

units.title: The idle gauge shows when a failover is over
units.claim: The idle gauge drops to zero during a failover and recovers as the pool refills, a quick way to confirm the failover has finished.

units.title: Set the pool together with the database's limits
units.claim: A pool makes connections cheap and bounded, but its size, timeouts and failover behaviour must be set together with the database's own limits.
mustPreserve: together with the database's own limits

mustNotClaim.claim: A bigger pool always makes queries faster.
mustNotClaim.why: The source says more connections slow every query once the database CPU is saturated.

mustNotClaim.claim: The statement timeout applies to every query, migrations included.
The pool reclaims leaked connections automatically.
mustNotClaim.why: The source says it never takes a leaked connection back by force.

mustNotClaim.claim: A sustained queue always means slow queries.
A failover is invisible to callers.
mustNotClaim.why: Requests may see POOL_EXHAUSTED for up to about 4 seconds.
